levelPages.answer: Sogda's step {step} teaches {words, plural, one {# German word} other {# German words}} and {topics, plural, one {# grammar topic} other {# grammar topics}}, the {half, select, first {first} other {second}} half of CEFR level {level}. cefr.A1: At A1 you understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases. You can introduce yourself, and ask and answer simple questions about where you live, people you know and things you have, as long as the other person speaks slowly and clearly.
cefr.A2: At A2 you understand sentences and frequent expressions about things that matter to you every day, such as family, shopping, where you live and work. You can handle simple, routine tasks that need a direct exchange of information.
cefr.B1: At B1 you understand the main points of clear, standard language about familiar things at work, school or in your free time. You can deal with most situations while travelling, and describe experiences, events, hopes and plans, with short reasons.
cefr.B2: At B2 you understand the main ideas of complex texts on concrete and abstract topics. You can talk with native speakers with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes it possible without strain for either side, and write clear, detailed texts that weigh the pros and cons of an issue.
cefr.C1: At C1 you understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts and recognise what they imply. You express yourself fluently and spontaneously, without searching for words, and use the language flexibly for social, academic and professional purposes.
cefr.C2: At C2 you understand virtually everything you hear or read. You can summarise information from different spoken and written sources, and express yourself spontaneously, very fluently and precisely, telling apart finer shades of meaning.

spaced-repetition.title: Spaced repetition with FSRS, explained | Sogda
spaced-repetition.description: How Sogda's {version} scheduler brings each German word back just before you'd forget it: rated Good, after {g1, number} days, then {g2, number}, {g3, number} and {g4, number}. Offline.
spaced-repetition.name: Spaced repetition
spaced-repetition.answer: Sogda plans every revision with {version}, a spaced-repetition method that brings each word back on the day your chance of recalling it would drop to {retention, number, percent}. A new word you rate Good comes back after {g1, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}, then after {g2, number}, {g3, number} and {g4, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} as you keep rating it Good, so your minutes go to the words you're about to forget.

what.heading: What FSRS is
what.body: FSRS, the Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler, is an open-source method for deciding when to revise. For each word it tracks how stable your memory of it is and how hard the word is for you, and from those it works out the day your chance of recalling it would drop to your target. Sogda runs {version} with its published default weights, on your phone.
what.target: Your target is {retention, number, percent} unless you change it: Target retention in Settings goes from {min, number, percent} to {max, number, percent}. A higher target brings words back sooner, so there are more revisions a day; a lower one spaces them further apart.

gaps.heading: The first gap depends on your rating
gaps.body: When a new word comes up, you rate how well you knew it with the app's four buttons. At the default target, the rating sets its first gap:
gaps.first: {rating}: back in {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}

chain.heading: Then the gaps grow
chain.body: Each time the word comes back and you rate it Good, your memory of it is more stable and the next gap is longer: {g1, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}, then {g2, number}, {g3, number} and {g4, number}, and after that {g5, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}, more than a year.
chain.lapse: Forget a word you'd learned and rate it Again, and FSRS lowers its stability: the word comes back sooner, and its gaps grow again from there.

plan.heading: Revision comes first, every day
plan.body: Each day's plan starts with revision: the words that are due, the earliest first, up to {revise, number} of them. When fewer are due, it fills the rest with the words you're most likely to have forgotten. Then come {new, number} new words, the grammar that's due and a few practice sentences.
plan.wait: Both numbers are defaults you can change in Settings. Due words beyond the day's {revise, number} wait for the next day, the earliest first, so a missed day never turns into a wall of revisions.

why.heading: Why your minutes go to the words you're about to forget
why.body: A word you know well is planned weeks or months ahead, so it takes none of today's time. A word that's fading is planned now, just before you'd forget it. The minutes you have each day go to the words that need them, and each revision you pass pushes the next one further out.

target.q: Can I change how often words come back?
target.a: Yes. Set Target retention in Settings, from {min, number, percent} to {max, number, percent}; the default is {retention, number, percent}. A higher target means shorter gaps and more revisions a day; a lower one, longer gaps and fewer.

missed.q: What happens if I miss a day?
missed.a: The words that were due wait for you. The next day's plan takes the earliest due first, up to {revise, number} revisions, and the rest follow on the days after. When you rate a word, FSRS counts the days that really passed.

offline.q: Does the scheduling need the internet?
offline.a: No. Sogda works fully offline: the scheduler runs on your phone, with no account, and your progress stays there.

grammar.a: Yes. Each grammar topic has its own schedule from the same scheduler, and comes back for practice when it's due.

compare.heading: How they compare with the Goethe and telc exams
compare.skills: The Goethe-Zertifikat and telc Deutsch exams test reading, listening, writing and speaking at each level. Sogda's papers share three of those skills, listening, writing and speaking, and add vocabulary, grammar, articles and word forms.
compare.reading: There's no reading-comprehension part: for reading, practise with longer German texts and the exams' own model papers.
compare.official: The papers are Sogda's own, generated from each step's words and grammar. They aren't official Goethe or telc papers, and their formats are Sogda's. The Goethe-Institut and telc publish model papers for every level on goethe.de and telc.net.

official.q: Are these official Goethe or telc exams?
official.a: No. They're Sogda's own papers, generated from each step's words and grammar. They share listening, writing and speaking with the real exams, have no reading part, and lead to no certificate.

reading.a: No. Sogda's papers have vocabulary, grammar, listening, writing and speaking sections. Practise reading with longer texts and the exams' own model papers.

sogda-vs-anki.title: Sogda or Anki for German: a ready course or your own decks
sogda-vs-anki.description: Sogda or Anki for German? Both use spaced repetition. Anki runs the decks you make or download; Sogda is a ready course, A1 to C2, offline.
sogda-vs-anki.name: Sogda or Anki
sogda-vs-anki.answer: Anki is a flashcard app: you make your own decks, or download decks other users have shared. Sogda is a ready German course from A1 to C2, with {words, number} words, {topics, number} grammar topics and {mocksPerStep, number} mock exams for every step, and both schedule your revision with spaced repetition.

body.p1: Both bring a card back just before you'd forget it. Anki's manual describes FSRS, the Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler, as an alternative to its older SM-2 algorithm that you can turn on (Anki 23.10 and later, AnkiDroid 2.17 and later). Sogda schedules every word with FSRS from the start.
Anki is the better fit when the cards are yours to make:

list.a: you want to make your own cards, for German or for anything else;
list.b: you already have a deck you trust, or want one from Anki's shared decks;
list.c: you want to set every scheduling option yourself;
list.d: you also study on a computer: Anki runs on Windows, Mac and Linux, with AnkiDroid on Android and AnkiMobile on iPhone.

body.p1: Sogda is the better fit when you want the course, not the cards:

list.a: you want the whole course ready, from your first “Hallo” to C2: {words, number} words, each with examples, its article and forms where it has them, and {topics, number} grammar topics, each with its rule and a short practice;
list.b: you want a plan for each day rather than decks to manage;
list.c: you want the meanings and a pronunciation guide in English, or in Bangla, Russian or Polish letters;
list.d: you're preparing for an exam: {mocksPerStep, number} mock exams for every step, with listening, writing and speaking, plus vocabulary and grammar;
list.e: you want it fully offline and with no account, on Android.

body.p1: Nothing stops you: take the course in Sogda, and keep an Anki deck for the words from your own work or studies that no course has.

Anki: its own manual at docs.ankiweb.net (Getting started; Deck options, on FSRS), read on 1 October 2026. Sogda: the app's course data. Anki is named here only to describe it; Sogda has no connection with it.

algorithm.a: Sogda uses FSRS, which Anki offers as an option from version 23.10; you turn it on in Anki's deck options. Anki's older SM-2 scheduler is what runs until you do.

import.q: Can I import my Anki deck into Sogda?
import.a: No. Sogda teaches its own course, so your Anki decks stay in Anki.

exam.q: Which is better for the Goethe or telc exam?
exam.a: With Anki, it depends on the deck. Sogda's steps are built around the exams, with {mocksPerStep, number} mock exams for every step that test listening, writing and speaking, plus vocabulary and grammar. They're not official papers, and there's no reading part.

iphone.a: Not yet: Sogda is on Android ({android} or newer), and iPhone is coming soon.

sogda-vs-duolingo.title: Sogda or Duolingo for German: how far, how deep, how offline
sogda-vs-duolingo.description: Sogda or Duolingo for German? Duolingo's German course goes through B2; Sogda goes A1 to C2 with grammar and mock exams, offline, no account.
sogda-vs-duolingo.name: Sogda or Duolingo
sogda-vs-duolingo.answer: Duolingo teaches many languages, and its German course goes through B2 on the CEFR scale, as Duolingo's blog said in April 2026. Sogda teaches only German, from A1 to C2 in {steps, number} steps, with {words, number} words, {topics, number} grammar topics and {mocksPerStep, number} mock exams for every step, fully offline and with no account.

body.p1: The CEFR has six levels, from A1 to C2. Duolingo's German course reaches B2, where you're an “independent user” of the language. Sogda's {steps, number} steps go on through C1 and C2, the levels of the Goethe-Zertifikat C1 and C2.
Duolingo is the better fit when German is one language among several:

list.a: you want to learn other languages in the same app;
list.b: B2 is as far as you need to go in German;
list.c: you're on iPhone today: Sogda is on Android only, for now.

body.p1: Sogda is the better fit when German is the goal:

list.a: you're aiming for C1 or C2, or for a Goethe or telc exam at any level: {mocksPerStep, number} mock exams for every step;
list.b: you want grammar as rules you can look up: {topics, number} topics, each with its rule and a short practice;
list.c: you want every word with its article and forms where it has them, examples, and a pronunciation guide in your meaning language's letters;
list.d: you learn from Bangla, Russian or Polish and want the meanings in your language;
list.e: you want it fully offline, with no account to make.

body.p1: Nothing stops you: one app for variety, another for depth. Sogda's plan takes as long as the daily goal you set, so it fits beside another app.

Duolingo: its blog post “Duolingo Course Content Can Take You to B2 Proficiency”, 22 April 2026, read on 1 October 2026. Sogda: the app's course data. Duolingo is named here only to describe it; Sogda has no connection with it.

levels.q: How far does Duolingo's German course go?
levels.a: Through B2 on the CEFR scale, according to Duolingo's blog in April 2026. Sogda goes on to C2.

exam.q: Which is better for the Goethe or telc exam?
exam.a: Sogda's steps are built around the exams, with {mocksPerStep, number} mock exams for every step that test listening, writing and speaking, plus vocabulary and grammar. They're not official papers, and there's no reading part.

Open the app and today's plan is there: revise what's due, learn a few new words, practise the grammar topic of the week, and read sentences made only from words you know. You set the daily goal and your rest days, and a reminder comes only when something is due.

Sogda schedules every word with FSRS, a modern spaced-repetition method. Each time you remember a word, the wait before it comes back grows, from days to weeks to months. Your time goes to the words you're about to forget.

{steps, number} steps from A1.1 to C2.2, with {words, number} words and {topics, number} grammar topics, each topic with its rule and a short practice. A short placement check starts you at the right step.

{mocksPerStep, number} mock exams for every step, {mocks, number} in all, with listening, writing and speaking like the real exams, plus vocabulary and grammar, and a result for each section. There's no reading-comprehension part. They're generated from the step's words and grammar: they aren't official Goethe or telc papers, and Sogda isn't affiliated with either.

Meanings in English, Bangla, Russian or Polish: one language, or two shown together. In Russian and Polish, the example sentences and grammar rules too. The app itself comes in English, Bangla, Polish or Russian.

Fully offline, with no account: your progress stays on your phone. The optional natural Supertonic voice is a one-time download of about 400 MB over Wi-Fi; otherwise Sogda uses your phone's German voice.
Android {android} or newer. iPhone: coming soon.
